headline: An audit of 394 adjacent-rank claims on the Open LLM Leaderboard finds 391 fail a significance test before any correction, and none survive once 27 unpublished sibling models are assumed.

items.title: Crystalline indium oxide hides 100× fewer subgap states than amorphous IZO
items.dek: Chen Wang and six co-authors compared transistors built from crystalline indium oxide against ones built from amorphous indium-zinc oxide, using magnetoresistance at low temperature to count the trap levels sitting inside the band gap, and report that the crystalline channel has more than two orders of magnitude fewer of them.
items.why_it_matters: Subgap states set how much gate voltage a transistor wastes between off and on, because every trap has to be filled before the Fermi level can move, and that stretched transition region is what forces a higher supply rail for the same drive current. For a transistor built up in the wiring stack rather than in the silicon beneath it, where the power budget is small and the temperature ceiling forbids the anneals that would heal defects, that is the binding constraint. The measurement route is the other half: reading trap density off a magnetoresistance curve is a check on the fitted transfer characteristic everyone currently uses, not a restatement of it.
items.background_md: Oxide semiconductors are the usual candidate for a transistor built above the copper wiring rather than in the silicon below it, because they can be deposited under the roughly 400 °C ceiling that copper and its surrounding low-k insulator impose, and because they leak very little when off. The cost is disorder. An amorphous film has no long-range order, so its conduction band edge is not sharp; it trails off into a tail of localised states inside the gap. Electrons in that tail do not travel in a band at all — they hop between localised sites, and how far they must hop sets the mobility.
items.deeper_md:
The method is the contribution as much as the result. Instead of fitting a subgap density of states out of a room-temperature transfer curve, the authors measure Hall effect and magnetoresistance across a range of temperatures. Down there the band tail conducts by variable-range hopping, and the magnetoresistance of a hopping system depends on the localisation radius of the sites being hopped between — so a field sweep returns a number for how tightly each trapped electron is held, and the subgap density of states follows from it.

Crystalline In₂O₃ comes out with a smaller localisation radius and a subgap density of states more than two orders of magnitude below amorphous IZO, which shows up as higher carrier mobility and a narrower transition region, and therefore a lower supply voltage for the same swing.

Two caveats. This is one group's devices with no independent replication, and the contrast is reported as a ratio rather than as absolute states per cubic centimetre per electronvolt, so the comparison is easier to trust than the level. Crystallinity is also not free: a December 2025 Stanford preprint reached 63 mV/dec and over 1 mA/µm with a channel-last gate-all-around device on an *amorphous* oxide, which is the bar a crystalline process has to clear while staying inside the same back-end thermal budget.

glossary.definition: The number of electronic states per unit energy per unit volume sitting inside the band gap, where a perfect crystal would have none. Each one must be filled before the gate can move the Fermi level further.

Conduction in which an electron tunnels between localised trap sites rather than travelling in a band, choosing hops that trade distance against energy difference. It dominates disordered films at low temperature.

The distance over which a trapped electron's wavefunction decays. Hopping rate falls exponentially with hop distance divided by this radius, so a smaller radius means a more tightly bound, less mobile carrier.
The gate voltage needed to change drain current tenfold. Room temperature puts a floor near 60 mV/decade, and traps in the gap push a real device above it.

items.fab_angle: Oxide semiconductors are one of the few channel materials a teaching cleanroom can actually deposit — reactive sputtering at low temperature, no epitaxy and no implanter. The transferable lesson here is about acceptance testing rather than deposition: a room-temperature transfer curve on a probe station will not separate two films whose trap densities differ by two orders of magnitude, so a group that wants to know whether its film improved needs a measurement that reaches into the gap.

items.title: Signed weights without interference, and backpropagation run on the chip
items.dek: Yuan Ren and four co-authors built a 16-by-16 optical matrix multiplier on thin-film lithium niobate that represents negative numbers directly, without relying on interference between light beams, and then ran the whole training loop on it — forward pass, error propagation and gradient computation all in the photonics.
items.why_it_matters: Optical matrix multipliers have been stuck between two bad options: coherent designs get signed arithmetic free from interference but need phase held stable across the whole chip, while incoherent designs are robust and then have to spend extra hardware per weight to express a minus sign. Doing signs natively in an incoherent path removes that per-weight overhead, so the cost of handling signs stops growing with matrix size. Closing the training loop in hardware matters for a separate reason: the weights being learned are then the weights the device actually implements, so modulator non-linearity and detector offset become part of what is fitted rather than an error the model must tolerate afterwards.
items.background_md: A matrix multiply dominates the arithmetic of a neural network, and it is a natural fit for optics: light passing through a set of attenuators and landing on a shared detector performs multiply-accumulate at the speed of whatever drives the modulators. Two things make it hard. Optical intensity cannot be negative, so a signed weight needs either interference between two phase-controlled beams or a second physical channel per weight. And training is normally done on a digital model of the device, so every mismatch between that model and the fabricated chip comes back as lost accuracy.
items.deeper_md:
The core is 16 × 16 with 256 channels, at 8-bit multiplication and 10-bit accumulation precision. The number that carries the claim is that tiling it up to a 256 × 256 matrix holds the 10-bit accumulation accuracy rather than degrading with tile count — tiling is how any fixed-size photonic core reaches a layer of realistic width, and accumulated tile error is where these demonstrations usually lose their precision. The loop demonstrated includes a nonlinearity and gradient computation on-chip, and the linear operations of a BERT-mini workload are executed on it.

The lineage sets what is actually new. The same platform produced a 120 GOPS tensor core in 2024 out of two lithium-niobate modulators, a III-V laser and a charge-integration photoreceiver, with a 60 GHz weight-update rate; and the same first author published a dual-wavelength incoherent signed scheme in May 2026 that puts complementary components on two wavelengths in a shared path, reporting four-quadrant multiplication to 1.27% standard deviation and over 40 GHz of modulation bandwidth. The new claim is that the sign-handling overhead per multiply-accumulate stays constant as the matrix grows.

What the preprint's abstract does not give is energy per operation, sustained throughput, or a comparison against a digital baseline at matched precision — and 8-bit multiply with 10-bit accumulate is well below what a transformer is normally trained in. Read it as evidence that in-hardware training works on this platform, not as a position on a performance curve.

glossary.definition: Computing with light intensities that do not interfere, so contributions add as powers on a detector. It tolerates phase drift, but intensity cannot go negative, which is why signs need special handling.

A wafer-scale platform with a sub-micron lithium niobate layer on oxide. The material's strong electro-optic effect lets an applied voltage change the refractive index fast enough for tens of gigahertz of modulation.
Computing the gradients used to update weights on the physical device itself rather than on a simulation of it, so each update already accounts for the hardware's real response.
A multiply that returns the correct sign for all four combinations of positive and negative input and weight — something an intensity-only optical path cannot do without extra encoding.

items.title: Both EDA vendors certify A14 flows two years before the node exists
items.dek: Synopsys and Cadence each said on 23 September that their digital and analog design flows are now certified on TSMC's A14, a 1.4-nanometre-class process that does not enter production until 2028, and Cadence adds that it has already taped out a 64 gigatransfer-per-second die-to-die interface block on it.
items.why_it_matters: A process node becomes usable not when the wafers work but when the design rules, the parasitic-extraction decks and the characterised cell libraries are stable enough that somebody will commit a mask set to them; tool certification is the public marker of that, and it is why an interface block rather than a processor is always the first thing taped out on a new node. The part that is new this round is the analog half. Synopsys names device-level routing automation on A14 as its milestone, and device-level routing — the wiring between the terminals of individual transistors — is the layer of analog layout that has stayed hand-drawn longest, because matching and parasitics there depend on exact geometry.
items.background_md: A logic node is advertised as three numbers — speed, power, density — but it is delivered as a process design kit: the geometric rules a layout must obey, SPICE models for the devices, decks that extract the parasitic resistance and capacitance of the wiring, and timing-characterised standard cells. None of it is usable until the tools that read it reproduce the foundry's own answers, which is what certification means in practice: the vendor runs the foundry's test cases through its flow and the foundry confirms the results match. Early versions of a kit change enough that a design started too soon has to be redone.
items.deeper_md:
What A14 is, in TSMC's own numbers from April 2025: against N2, up to 15% more speed at the same power or up to 30% less power at the same speed, and more than 20% higher logic density, with production in 2028. It does *not* carry backside power — TSMC's Super Power Rail arrives on A12 in 2029, per the April 2026 symposium release, which also put A13 in 2029 at 6% area saving versus A14 with design rules fully backward compatible with it. So an A14 design still spends front-side metal tracks on power distribution.

Cadence's certified list is the digital flow enumerated tool by tool — Genus, Innovus, Cerebrus, Tempus, Quantus, Voltus, Pegasus, Liberate, EMX — plus Virtuoso Studio for custom and analog, and it claims up to 2.5× fewer design iterations on automated migration to A16 and A14. It reports UCIe-64G taped out on A14, and DDR5, LPDDR5 and PCIe 6.0 IP taped out on N2P. Synopsys reports certified digital and analog flows, device routing enablement on A14, and integrated-voltage-regulator co-design on CoWoS in its 3DIC Compiler.

Every one of those is a vendor statement about its own work against a preliminary design kit, and none of it is independently checkable. TSMC's PPA figures are likewise TSMC's, quoted against its own N2 baseline.

glossary.definition: The foundry's delivery to designers: geometric design rules, device models, parasitic-extraction decks and characterised standard cells. A node is only as usable as its kit is mature.
The moment a finished layout is released for mask-making. It is irreversible and expensive, which makes it the honest test of whether anyone believes a node's design kit yet.
The chiplet die-to-die interface standard, running here at 64 gigatransfers per second per lane — the electrical link between two dies inside one package rather than between two packages on a board.

Routing power rails on the underside of the wafer instead of down through the signal-wiring stack, which frees front-side metal tracks and cuts IR drop. TSMC calls its version Super Power Rail; A14 does not have it.

items.fab_angle: Cadence's certification list is effectively a digital flow named one stage at a time: synthesis, placement and routing, clock and timing signoff, extraction, power integrity, physical verification, and library characterisation. That is the same sequence a student flow runs on an open PDK, so the list is a usable map of what a tapeout actually requires. What changes at A14 is that the decks are proprietary and analog device routing is being automated too — the hand-drawn analog layout still taught as a craft is being squeezed from below.

items.title: 52 hardware fuzzers, and only 12 take guidance from a security property
items.dek: G Abarajithan and six co-authors read all 52 published hardware fuzzers — tools that fire randomised stimulus at a chip design in simulation before any masks are cut — and find that 32 of them steer on structural coverage of the design's own logic, while only 12 steer on a security property.
items.why_it_matters: A fuzzing campaign can only find a failure it can reach, recognise and prioritise before its compute budget runs out, and those three are controlled by three different things: the input generator, the oracle, and the guidance signal. Steering on line or toggle coverage optimises reachability alone and says nothing about recognition, which is how a tool reports strong coverage and still misses the bug class it was bought for. The immediate practical consequence is that the published numbers do not compare — the survey finds few of these fuzzers benchmarked against modern constrained-random verification at all, and most name their target design without naming its revision.
items.background_md: Verification, not design, consumes most of the engineering effort on a large chip, because a bug found after masks exist costs a respin. The standard method is constrained-random verification: generate legal stimulus at random inside a hand-written constraint model, run it against a reference implementation, and watch coverage until it stops moving. Fuzzing is the software world's answer to the same problem — mutate inputs and let a feedback signal push the mutation toward unexplored behaviour — and importing it to hardware forces a choice about what that feedback signal should be when the thing under test is a state machine rather than a program.
items.deeper_md:
The census: 52 fuzzers, of which 31 target CPUs, 10 target IP blocks, 9 target SoC or network-on-chip, and 3 are miscellaneous. Of the 44 with an identifiable oracle, 21 compare against a reference model, 13 use property or runtime checkers, 11 are differential or relational, and 8 use a specialised semantic model; eight more hand the oracle to the user and six report reachability with no pass/fail at all. On guidance, 32 use the implementation's own structure — control flow, mux toggles, register state — of which 24 chase coverage novelty and 8 optimise a numeric score.

The artifact count is the part that bounds everything else. Among CPU fuzzers, 20 release public code, 4 publish placeholders and 5 report artifacts as unavailable; among SoC fuzzers only 2 publish infrastructure; among IP fuzzers 4 release code and 7 release nothing, several requiring commercial ATPG or synthesis licences to reproduce at all.

An SoK is a reading of a literature, not a measurement, and the categories are the authors' own — a tool can sit in two. The paper also tabulates no aggregate bug counts, which is itself the finding. A second systematisation a month earlier, ARCUS, arrived at a compatible complaint from a different angle, calling for standardised evaluation metrics and scalable reference models.

glossary.definition: The industry-standard method: randomly generate stimulus inside a hand-written legality model, compare the design's response against a reference implementation, and track coverage until it stops improving.
The part of a test that decides whether what happened counts as a failure. Without one, a campaign reports only where it went, not whether anything there was wrong.
The fraction of a design's signals observed switching in both directions during a run. It is cheap to measure, and it tells you a wire moved, not that the logic around it behaved correctly.
Whether the code and data behind a paper are published so the result can be re-run. The survey's count of which fuzzers did is what limits every cross-tool comparison it can make.

items.title: A 17-cycle decompression penalty turns a compressed cache into a channel
items.dek: David K. Oh and Hiroshi Sasaki show that the XOR cache — a last-level cache design that stores two lines as their bitwise XOR to nearly double effective capacity — leaks, because recovering one of a compressed pair takes 17 cycles longer than an ordinary hit, enough to carry 2.9 megabits per second between two colluding processes.
items.why_it_matters: Cache covert channels have until now been built out of capacity: the sender evicts lines and the receiver notices they are gone, at the cost of a whole set of evictions per bit. Encoding in compression state instead puts one bit on one line, so a single cache set carries several bits at once and the traffic per bit collapses — from about 52.8 last-level misses down to 0.38 in the authors' simulation, which is also what makes the channel quiet enough to be hard to detect. The general lesson outruns this one design: compression makes the space a line occupies depend on its data, and any structure whose timing depends on a neighbour's data is a channel.
items.background_md: Caches are shared, and sharing is what makes them leak. If two processes use the same cache, the time one takes to read memory depends on what the other did. The classic construction, Prime+Probe, fills a cache set, waits, and re-reads it: a slow access means the victim evicted something, which is one bit. Everything about that attack follows from the cache being an occupancy-limited resource, and every defence built against it assumes as much. Compressed caches change the resource itself — the space a line takes now depends on the data in it.
items.deeper_md:
The XOR cache stores two lines A and B as A⊕B, exploiting the data already duplicated between private caches and the shared last level. Reading a compressed line goes through the coherence protocol by one of three paths — local recovery, direct forwarding, or remote recovery — and they do not cost the same. The sender encodes a 1 by writing to A, which drives that line to Modified state and breaks the pair, leaving B standalone and fast to fetch; it encodes a 0 by doing nothing, leaving the pair intact so the receiver's read has to go the remote-recovery route. Measured medians: 122 cycles standalone against 139 cycles for remote recovery, a 17-cycle gap made of directory indirection, network-on-chip hops and a cache-to-cache transfer.

In full-system gem5/Ruby — two 3 GHz out-of-order x86 cores, 32 KiB L1D, 256 KiB L2, 1 MiB per-core 16-way LLC at 40-cycle latency — the channel runs at 2,886.7 Kbps with a 0.982% bit error rate over 50,000 bits, against Prime+Probe at 220.2 Kbps and 0.910%.

Two limits worth stating plainly. This is simulation, not silicon, and the XOR cache is an ISCA 2025 research proposal rather than a shipping design, so nothing currently deployed is affected. The authors also note that a different line-pairing policy would force the attacker to reverse-engineer the pairing relation without removing the timing primitive underneath it; their own suggested fixes are protection-domain tags that block cross-domain pairing, or padding standalone hits to constant time.

glossary.definition: The largest and slowest cache on the die, shared by every core. Being shared is exactly what lets it carry information between processes that were never meant to communicate.
A deliberate communication path between two cooperating processes that the system's isolation was supposed to prevent — as distinct from a side channel, where the leaking party is unaware.
The standard cache attack: fill a cache set, let the other process run, then time re-reads to see which lines were evicted. Each bit costs a full set of evictions, which is why it is slow and noisy.
The coherence-protocol tag meaning one core holds the only copy of a line and has dirtied it. Writing to a line drives it here, which in this design is what splits a compressed pair apart.

items.title: 391 of 394 leaderboard rank claims fail before correcting for anything
items.dek: Chen Yang, Xianyang Zhang and Jun Chen audited 394 adjacent-rank comparisons on Hugging Face's Open LLM Leaderboard — each one the claim that a model beats the model directly below it — and found 391 fail a significance test even before accounting for sibling models a provider evaluated and never published.
items.why_it_matters: The trouble is not that benchmark scores are noisy but that neither the noise nor the number of attempts behind a published score is reported, and the correction depends on both. Because a provider's variants are correlated with one another, 27 hidden siblings demand the same critical value as somewhere between about 55 and 1,900 independent tries depending on how correlated they are — so the size of the correction hinges on a quantity nobody publishes. The authors' answer is to invert the question: instead of correcting for an unknown number of hidden attempts, report how much hidden selection a given claim could survive, which is a number a reader can check.
items.background_md: A leaderboard rank is a comparison between two averages over a finite set of test items, so each number carries sampling error, and a margin smaller than that error is not evidence of anything. Two further effects compound it. Items within a benchmark are not independent — a model good at one subject tends to be good at the next — so the effective sample is smaller than the item count suggests. And a provider that evaluates several checkpoints and publishes the best has performed a selection, which inflates the winner's apparent margin: the multiple-comparisons problem that forces corrections in any field running many tests at once.
items.deeper_md:
The board audited covers six benchmarks and 28,659 evaluation items. Across the 394 adjacent-rank claims the median standardised margin is z = 0.17, and only 3 clear the uncorrected threshold at all. Applying the Gaussian correction at 27 hidden variants with a within-family correlation floor of 0.56 leaves zero certified; the top-ranked claim, at z = 2.61, would need a correlation floor of at least 0.849 under the fully adjusted treatment to survive at that k.

The mechanism behind the correction is where the paper is most useful. The selected margin — best-of-my-variants minus the comparator — follows a one-factor Dunnett distribution under the null, and its critical value is governed by the correlation between sibling models. Crucially that correlation depends on the sampling model, not just on the family: weighting items by count gives 0.90, because MMLU's 14,042 items dominate; weighting to match the leaderboard's equal-weight composite gives 0.46 for the same family, because GSM8K's 1,319 items then supply 91% of the variance; resampling MMLU subjects as blocks gives 0.92. Only the score-matched 0.46 governs the critical value, and using the wrong one is how a claim looks certified.

The authors bound their own result: Gaussian tails assumed, verdicts are pair-conditional and marked metadata-insufficient wherever private candidate logs are unavailable, and the guarantee covers selection inside a fixed family — not generating new candidates from benchmark feedback, which is the harder case.

glossary.definition: The assertion that the model at rank n genuinely beats the model at rank n+1. It is the weakest claim a leaderboard makes, which is what makes it the fair thing to test.
A score difference divided by its standard error. As a rule of thumb, |z| below about 2 means the gap sits inside what resampling the test set alone would produce.

The inflation of an apparent winner's margin when several candidates were evaluated and only the best was published. Correcting for it requires knowing how many were tried, which providers do not disclose.
The reference distribution for the largest of several correlated comparisons against one common control — exactly the shape of "the best of my variants versus the model below me".

foundations.topic: The Intel 4004 and the first microprocessors
foundations.subtitle: A calculator chip that became a general-purpose computer, and the sixteen pins that shaped it.
foundations.tldr: In 1971 Intel delivered a four-chip set for a Japanese desk calculator, and one of the four was a complete central processor on a single piece of silicon: 2,300 transistors in 12 square millimetres, drawn at a 10 micrometre minimum line width on 2-inch wafers. It was slower and narrower than the wired-up logic it replaced, and it won anyway, because one design could be aimed at a different product by changing the contents of a read-only memory instead of redrawing masks. Almost every decision inside it traces back to two constraints: the package it had to fit, and the process that could be made to yield.

sections.heading: The job was to avoid drawing a dozen custom chips
sections.body_md:
Busicom came to Intel wanting a set of custom integrated circuits for a printing calculator. Ted Hoff proposed something different: a general-purpose four-bit computer built from four chips, with the calculator's behaviour living in a read-only memory rather than in the wiring.

That is an engineering argument, not a sales one. Random logic drawn for one product has to be redesigned and re-masked for the next, and every mask layer is a fixed cost paid before a single good die exists. A stored-program machine moves the difference between products into the contents of one memory. The price is time: an operation that hardwired logic completes in a single pass now takes several instruction cycles, each of which is several clock periods.

The four chips became the MCS-4 set — the 4004 processor, the 4001 ROM, the 4002 RAM, and the 4003 shift register — and the first thing they ran was the Busicom 141-PF printing calculator.

sections.heading: Sixteen pins, and the rest follows
sections.body_md:
The 4004 shipped in a standard 16-pin dual in-line package. Subtract power and ground and you are left with roughly eleven pins for the entire system bus plus every input and output. There is no version of a separate address bus and data bus that fits.

So the 4004 has one four-bit bus, and it sends addresses and data down it at different times. Reading one instruction takes eight clock periods in a fixed pattern: three to push out the twelve address bits four at a time, two to fetch the instruction back, three to execute. Twelve address bits is 4,096 locations, which is where the 4 kilobyte program limit comes from — not from ambition, from pin count.

At the minimum clock period of 1.35 microseconds — 740 kilohertz — eight periods is 10.8 microseconds per instruction, or roughly 100,000 instructions per second. Every architectural number in the part is downstream of the package.
sections.deeper_md: The eight phases carry names in the documentation: A1, A2, A3 for the three address nibbles, M1 and M2 for the two instruction-fetch nibbles, and X1, X2, X3 for execution. Several instructions are two words long and therefore take two complete cycles, 21.6 µs. This is the cost of multiplexing made visible: a machine with separate 12-bit address and 8-bit data buses would have needed about 20 more pins and could have fetched in one period instead of five.

sections.heading: Silicon gate is what made one chip out of it
sections.body_md:
The process mattered as much as the architecture. In a conventional MOS transistor the aluminium gate is patterned after the source and drain, so it has to be drawn wide enough to overlap them even when the two masks misalign, and that deliberate overlap is wasted area and wasted capacitance.

Silicon gate technology inverts the order. The gate is polycrystalline silicon, patterned first, and then it acts as its own mask for the source and drain doping. The two are aligned by construction rather than by the alignment accuracy of a machine — the property that gives the technique its name, self-alignment. The Computer History Museum's summary of what that bought is blunt: three to five times the speed in half the chip area of conventional MOS.

Federico Faggin had built the first commercial silicon-gate integrated circuit at Fairchild in 1968, then Intel's 1101 memory in 1969. The 4004 was the third generation of the same process idea.

sections.heading: Four bits, because the arithmetic was decimal
sections.body_md:
A calculator works in decimal, and one decimal digit packs into four bits as binary-coded decimal. A four-bit datapath is therefore the natural width for the job, and the 4004's instruction set includes decimal as well as binary arithmetic to suit it.

The register file is sixteen four-bit registers plus an accumulator, and subroutine returns are held in a three-level on-chip stack — three, not an arbitrary depth, because each level is real flip-flops competing for the same 12 square millimetres. There are 46 instructions in total, covering arithmetic, subroutine call and return, data-memory transfers and I/O.

Notice that the pin constraint and the application constraint point the same way. Four bits is what the package could carry and four bits is what a decimal digit needs, so nothing had to be traded. That coincidence is rare, and it is part of why a calculator chip turned out to be a usable general-purpose part.

sections.heading: The processor is the least interesting chip in the set
sections.body_md:
A central processor with no memory and no way to reach the outside world computes nothing, which is why Intel sold the MCS-4 as a set rather than selling the 4004.

The 4001 is a 256 by 8-bit mask-programmable ROM with four I/O lines attached. The 4002 holds 320 bits of RAM, organised as four banks of twenty characters, plus four output lines. The 4003 is a ten-bit serial-to-parallel shift register that exists purely to turn a few processor pins into many slow outputs — keyboard scanning, printer solenoids, lamps.

The word mask-programmable is doing quiet work there. The program is a mask layer, so changing the software still means a mask change and a fabrication run. What the architecture bought was not free software; it was cutting the number of product-specific masks from a whole custom logic set down to one memory layer.
sections.deeper_md: The division of labour also explains the I/O pins scattered across the memory chips rather than concentrated on the processor. With eleven usable pins on the 4004, there was nowhere to put general-purpose I/O; putting four lines on each ROM and RAM chip meant that a system's I/O capability grew automatically as its memory grew, which is exactly the scaling a calculator needs.

sections.heading: What it cost, and why anyone took the trade
sections.body_md:
Judged as a calculator engine the 4004 is a poor part: 100,000 instructions per second, four bits wide, 4 kilobytes of program space, several cycles for work that dedicated logic did in one. A team willing to draw the custom chips would have got a faster, cheaper calculator.

What they would not have got is a second product. The trade is design effort and mask count against performance, and for anyone shipping more than one thing it is a good trade — which is the argument the whole industry eventually accepted.

It is also worth being accurate about primacy. Four-Phase Systems' AL1 slice dates from 1969 and the MP944 chip set built for an aircraft computer from 1970, both before the 4004 reached customers. What the 4004 had that they did not was that it was sold to anybody, as a documented catalogue part, with memory and I/O chips designed to sit beside it.

glossary.definition: Making the transistor gate from polycrystalline silicon and patterning it before the source and drain, so the gate masks its own doping step. The source, drain and gate end up aligned by construction rather than by mask alignment accuracy.

MOS logic built only from p-channel transistors, with a resistive or transistor load. It was the process that could be made to yield in 1971; it is slower and burns static power compared with the complementary CMOS that replaced it.

One set of wires carrying different information at different times — here addresses during three clock phases and instruction data during two. It trades clock cycles for pins, which is the right trade when pins are the scarce resource.
Read-only memory whose contents are fixed by one photomask during fabrication. The program is therefore a manufacturing step, not a file, and changing it requires a new mask and a new wafer run.

Storing each decimal digit in its own four bits rather than converting the whole number to binary. It wastes six of sixteen codes per digit and in exchange makes decimal arithmetic and decimal display trivial.

The full sequence of clock periods needed to fetch and execute one instruction — eight on the 4004, so 10.8 µs at its 740 kHz maximum clock. It is the unit that actually sets how fast a machine runs, not the clock frequency.

foundations.try_this: The 4004's minimum line width was 10 µm and its die was 12 mm² — both comfortably inside what MNF's maskless stepper and teaching cleanroom are being built to reach. Lay out a single p-channel MOS inverter to 10 µm design rules, expose it, and measure the printed linewidth against the drawn one on the profilometer; the difference is your process bias, and absorbing it is what every design rule in a real PDK exists to do. Then open the timing section of the University of Hamburg MCS-4 overview cited below and hand-count the eight clock phases of one instruction, so the 10.8 µs number stops being a specification and becomes something you derived.
